title: Heavy-Tailed Dispersal Kernels from Stopped Subdiffusive Fractional Brownian Motion
authors: Luis F. Gordillo, Priscilla E. Greenwood
abstract: Subdiffusive fractional Brownian motions produce localized aggregation when particles are stopped at exponentially distributed times. In applications where clumping and long-distance dispersal events are observed simultaneously, such as in some instances of seed dispersal, this model fails to describe the tails of the data. The resulting redistribution kernel has only an exponentially decaying tail, whereas a heavier tail is needed for modeling the long-distance dispersal observed. Here we propose a model in which subdiffusive particles stop at exponentially distributed times, but with a rate parameter that is Gamma distributed. This heterogeneity in stopping rates causes the density of final radial positions to have a heavy-tailed distribution. Our model retains the strong localized clumping characteristic of subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion while simultaneously generating the heavy tails required for realistic long-distance dispersal.
summary: This paper proposes a refined model for particle dispersal by combining subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion with stopping times whose rates are drawn from a Gamma distribution. This heterogeneity successfully generates the heavy-tailed power-law decay necessary to describe rare, long-distance events while retaining the localized clumping characteristic of the underlying subdiffusion process.
main_problem: To develop a model for dispersal kernels that accurately describe both localized clumping and rare, long-distance dispersal events by generating heavy tails.
main_result: By introducing heterogeneity in the stopping rate (making it Gamma-distributed), the resulting radial density function exhibits a power-law decay $g(r) \sim r^{-1 - a/H}$, confirming a heavy-tailed distribution.
method: The analysis involves deriving and performing asymptotic analysis on the radial probability density function by combining subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion (fBm) with randomized exponential stopping times.
model_or_system: The system models particle dispersal using subdiffusive fBm ($H < 1/2$) where the stopping time rate ($\lambda$) is drawn from a Gamma distribution. This combination generates the required heavy-tailed statistics for realistic environmental modeling.
key_observables: Radial probability density function $g(r)$ and its tail behavior, specifically the power-law decay $r^{-1 - a/H}$ as $r 	o \infty$.
important_parameters: Hurst exponent ($H$), Gamma distribution parameters ($a, b$), and the diffusion parameter ($\sigma$). The regime of interest is subdiffusion ($0 < H < 1/2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations valid in the large-$r$ limit (e.g., $t \gg b$) and assumes that the underlying movement follows fBm.
figures_summary: Figures compare simulation results for randomized vs. constant stopping rates, showing clear heavy tails only when rate randomization is included. Hill plots and Mean-excess plots are used to diagnose this tail behavior.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the failure of simple models (exponential decay) for long-distance dispersal, proposes randomizing the stopping rate parameter ($\lambda \sim 	ext{Gamma}$), derives the asymptotic power-law tail $g(r) \sim r^{-1 - a/H}$, and validates this result through both analytical methods and numerical simulations.
why_interesting: While focused on physical dispersal, the mathematical techniques used—analyzing heavy tails arising from multiplicative noise or randomized rates in anomalous diffusion processes—are highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics problems involving complex particle interactions or energy dissipation.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Radial distribution of stopped paths of a subdiffusive fBm with randomized stopping rate λ ∼ Gamma(a, b). (a) Stopped positions, (b) Histogram of stopping distances. The diagnostic plots: Hill (c), Mean-excess (d) and Log-log survival (e), consistently support the presence of a heavy tail in the distribution of radial distances, see text.

Figure 2: Same plot as Figure (1) but with constant stopping rate λ = 1. Notice the difference in scale from Figure (1), see also Figure (3). The diagnostic plots (c), (d) and (e) support the absence of a heavy tail.
Figure 3: Scatter plots in Figure (1)a (red) and Figure (2)a (blue) superposed for comparison.
